title: How Many Species Is It Worth?

scenes.visual: Title card 'How Many Species Is It Worth?' over two small dot grids. COLOUR MAP, same in both films: species 1 TEAL, species 2 GOLD, species 3 VIOLET, species 4 CORAL dots; the effective number is always a row of identical NAVY 'equal species' columns; the order dial is a semicircle labelled q = 0, 1, 2; on the shore, Ulva GREEN, barnacles GREY, Gigartina RED. Cream background, 16:9. Every number appears only as on-screen text. Effective numbers are computed (label 'computed'); anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: Two plots hold the same four species, a hundred individuals each. Can one be more diverse than the other? Count the species, and they tie. Look at the dots, and they do not look alike.
scenes.visual: Two 10x10 grids of 100 dots, labelled 'plot A' and 'plot B'. Plot A: 25 teal, 25 gold, 25 violet, 25 coral, scattered. Plot B: 40 teal, 40 gold, 10 violet, 10 coral, scattered. A tally 'species: 4' appears under each, then an equals sign between them, then a question mark.
scenes.narration: Two plots hold the same four species, a hundred individuals each. Can one be more diverse than the other? Count the species, and they tie. Look at the dots, and they do not look alike.

scenes.tts: Richness is the number of species present. Both plots have four, so richness calls it a tie. But richness counts every species once, however rare it is. It ignores abundance entirely.
scenes.visual: One dot of each colour lifts out of each grid into a row of four, labelled 'richness S = 4' under both. In plot B, the lone violet and coral dots blink to show they stand for only 10 individuals each, yet count fully.
scenes.narration: Richness is the number of species present. Both plots have four, so richness calls it a tie. But richness counts every species once, however rare it is. It ignores abundance entirely.

scenes.tts: Diversity also asks how evenly the individuals are shared. In plot A, every species holds the same share. In plot B, two species hold most of the individuals, and two are rare.
scenes.visual: The dots of each grid slide down into a bar chart of relative abundance, colour by species. Plot A: four equal bars at 0.25. Plot B: teal and gold bars at 0.4, violet and coral at 0.1. Axis 'share of individuals'.
scenes.narration: Diversity also asks how evenly the individuals are shared. In plot A, every species holds the same share. In plot B, two species hold most of the individuals, and two are rare.

scenes.tts: Here is a way to put richness and evenness on one scale. Imagine a community in which every species is equally common. How many such species would score the same as plot B? That count is the effective number of species.
scenes.visual: Beside plot B's bar chart, a row of identical NAVY columns grows one at a time; a balance scale between them tips until it levels at a little over three columns, the last column only partly filled. Label 'effective number of species: how many equally common species give the same value'. Schematic balance; the level point is computed.
scenes.narration: Here is a way to put richness and evenness on one scale. Imagine a community in which every species is equally common. How many such species would score the same as plot B? That count is the effective number of species.

scenes.tts: For plot A, the answer is four, the same as its richness. For plot B, it is fewer than four, because two species hold most of the individuals.
scenes.visual: Plot A's navy row: 4 full columns, on screen '4.00'. Plot B's navy row: about 3.3 columns, on screen '3.30 (order 1, computed)'. Plot B's two tall bars pulse beside its row.
scenes.narration: For plot A, the answer is four, the same as its richness. For plot B, it is fewer than four, because two species hold most of the individuals.

scenes.tts: The measure has a dial, called the order. At order zero, every species counts once, however rare. As the order rises, common species count for more, and rare ones for less.
scenes.visual: A semicircular dial labelled q = 0, 1, 2 appears above the two navy rows. At q = 0 a caption reads 'order 0 = richness S'. The needle starts at 0.
scenes.narration: The measure has a dial, called the order. At order zero, every species counts once, however rare. As the order rises, common species count for more, and rare ones for less.

scenes.tts: Turn the dial for plot B. Its row of equal species shrinks, step by step, as its two rare species count for less. Plot A does not move, because nothing in it is rare.
scenes.visual: Needle sweeps q = 0 to 1 to 2. Plot B's navy row shrinks: 4.00 to 3.30 to 2.94 (computed, shown on screen as 'order 0: 4', 'order 1: 3.30', 'order 2: 2.94'). In plot B's bar chart the violet and coral bars fade as q rises. Plot A's row stays at 4.00 at every setting.
scenes.narration: Turn the dial for plot B. Its row of equal species shrinks, step by step, as its two rare species count for less. Plot A does not move, because nothing in it is rare.

scenes.tts: So the order you choose changes the number. At order zero, the effective number is just the richness, so plot B ties plot A. Above order zero, it equals the richness only when every species is equally common. Always say which order you used.
scenes.visual: A label card stamps onto plot B's row: 'effective number, order 2'. A banner: 'order 0: always = richness S. Above order 0: = S only when all species are equally common'. Small notes: 'higher orders: discount rare species'.
scenes.narration: So the order you choose changes the number. At order zero, the effective number is just the richness, so plot B ties plot A. Above order zero, it equals the richness only when every species is equally common. Always say which order you used.

scenes.tts: Now swap plot B's colours, so the rare species become the common ones. Nothing changes. These indices use only counts, never names, so none of them sees which species are present.
scenes.visual: In plot B's grid, teal and gold dots swap colours with violet and coral (now 40 violet, 40 coral, 10 teal, 10 gold). The navy row and every on-screen value stay exactly where they were; a label 'count-based indices: blind to identity'.
scenes.narration: Now swap plot B's colours, so the rare species become the common ones. Nothing changes. These indices use only counts, never names, so none of them sees which species are present.

scenes.tts: One last test. A storm sweeps through plot B and kills the same share of every species. Most individuals die. What happens to its effective number?
scenes.visual: A storm cloud passes over plot B; nine of every ten dots of each colour grey out and vanish, leaving 4 teal, 4 gold, 1 violet, 1 coral. On screen: 'same share killed in every species'. The navy row pulses with a question mark.
scenes.narration: One last test. A storm sweeps through plot B and kills the same share of every species. Most individuals die. What happens to its effective number?

scenes.visual: Hold the frame; a 5-second countdown; caption 'Predict: up, down or unchanged?'.

scenes.tts: Nothing happens to it. The counts drop, but every species keeps the same share. So the effective number stays exactly where it was.
scenes.visual: The surviving dots slide into a bar chart: shares 0.4, 0.4, 0.1, 0.1, identical to before. The navy row stays at 3.30 and 2.94 (computed). Label 'counts fell; shares did not'.
scenes.narration: Nothing happens to it. The counts drop, but every species keeps the same share. So the effective number stays exactly where it was.

scenes.tts: So a disturbance can change diversity in only two ways. It can change which species are present. Or it can change how evenly the individuals are shared, as the survivors regrow. Whether that raises or lowers diversity is a question for experiments.
scenes.visual: Two arrows lead into the navy row, labelled 'who is present' and 'how evenly they are shared'; a third arrow labelled 'killing the same share of all' is crossed out. Then a small tag 'raise or lower? test it' appears beside a beaker and a boulder icon.
scenes.narration: So a disturbance can change diversity in only two ways. It can change which species are present. Or it can change how evenly the individuals are shared, as the survivors regrow. Whether that raises or lowers diversity is a question for experiments.

scenes.visual: Hex end card. Take-home line: 'Diversity is how many equally common species a community is worth.'
